howto.title: How to read this paper
howto.intro:
What our teachers reported about how our standards are taught, K-12. Eight parts: the whole school, the three grade bands and the four subjects. Each part opens with the picture (curricular capacity, grade by grade), then Facts, Patterns and Moving forward, five items each.

**Where the numbers come from.** The ratings sheet of 9 November 2026 (2,166 standards, 2,709 ratings), checked against the Vertical Alignment reports.

**The three ratings.**

| Rating | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Taught in depth | ALL classes in the grade consistently teach, reteach, review and assess the standard |
| Introduced / exposed | Anything in between (for example, 3 of 5 classes) |
| Not taught | No class in the grade teaches it |

**Keep in mind.**

- The ratings report teaching across a whole grade, not what students know, and they judge no one.
- "In depth" is all or nothing. Teams may have read it more or less strictly.
- Much literacy is also taught in Science and Social Studies, and may not show in the ELA ratings.
- Shares are of grade-level ratings. Essential Elements are counted apart.

**Curricular capacity.** What an average grade reports taking to depth, introducing or not teaching in a year. Not a target: we cannot teach everything equally, so we choose the mix on purpose.

**Categories.** Each item carries a small label (for example Bright spots, Gaps, Handoffs), the same set in every part, so a team can follow one kind of observation across parts.

whole.title: Part 1. The whole school, K-12
whole.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 63% of our grade-level ratings are at least introduced, and 23% are taught in depth.

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All subjects | 1,754 | 23% | 40% | 37% |
| Math | 460 | 17% | 45% | 38% |
| ELA | 652 | 35% | 44% | 21% |
| Science | 247 | 35% | 23% | 42% |
| Social Studies | 395 | 4% | 36% | 60% |

items.title: ELA carries more than half of all depth.
items.text: 227 of the 406 in-depth ratings are ELA (56%). Depth is highest in Science Grade 10 (79% in depth), then ELA Grade 2 (71%) and ELA Grade 7 (70%).

items.title: Standards not taught in their own grade.
items.text: 281 standards are rated not taught in their own grade (or, for standards shared across grades, by every grade that shares them). A further 172 are rated not taught in the grade or course where they fit.

items.title: Progressions and hand-overs between schools.
items.text: 59 of 155 progressions break down on an official link. 46 standards taught in depth build on a standard rated not taught in an earlier school: 3 on official links (all Math), 43 on suggested links.

items.title: Introduced, never in depth.
items.text: 581 standards are introduced in at least one grade and in depth in none (Math 186, ELA 241, Science 49, Social Studies 105).

items.title: Fifteen places to start a conversation about depth.
items.text: Each rated all its standards, and none in depth: Math in Grades 3, 6, 7 and 8; ELA in Kindergarten and Grade 3; Science in Grade 1; Social Studies in Grades 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10 and 12.

items.title: Coverage is steady; depth does not climb with grade.
items.text: Every band at least introduces 61% to 63% of its standards. Grade 2 (55% in depth) is the highest grade in the school, and Grade 12 (23%) sits level with Grade 5 (24%).

items.title: Each change of school shifts depth by subject.
items.text: From Grade 5 to Grade 6, Math falls (32% to 0%) while ELA rises (18% to 40%). From Grade 8 to Grade 9, Math rises (0% to 30%) while ELA (50% to 33%) and Science (43% to 17%) fall.

items.title: Essential Elements are rated in depth far more often.
items.text: 43% of Essential Element ratings are in depth, against 23% of main standards (in K-5, 56% against 21%). Much in-depth teaching may sit at the Essential Element level, or teams may have rated the support they give.

items.title: Grade 2 and Grade 3 rated very differently.
items.text: Grade 2 is 10 points or more above its subjects' averages in Math, ELA and Science; Grade 3 is 10 or more below in all three. A whole grade moving together suggests a shared cause (how the scale was read, time, staffing).

items.title: Priority standards are deeper in secondary; level in K-5.
items.text: Priority standards are in depth more often than all standards in 6-8 (32% against 20%) and 9-12 (38% against 28%). In K-5 the power standards (20%) are level with all standards (21%).
Which standards matter most for our students to reach in depth, given where they start, and do we agree on that list across K-12?
items.data: 581 standards introduced and never in depth; 676 priority and power ratings below in depth
items.step: We could agree a short, shared K-12 list of standards every class takes to depth, starting with priority or power standards now rated introduced.

items.text: Where are vocabulary, speaking and writing taught in Science and Social Studies, and how could those lessons count toward our ELA standards?
items.data: ELA Language is 10% in depth in K-5; the literacy audit found about two-fifths of vocabulary and speaking work outside the literacy block
items.step: We could map where vocabulary, speaking and writing are taught in Science and Social Studies units, and count those lessons toward our ELA standards.

items.text: For one progression in your subject that breaks down, what would the grade below need to teach, and what would the grade above need to check on arrival?
items.data: 10 of the 59 progressions that break down are in Math, and 4 of those trace back to Grade 3 standards rated not taught
items.step: We could take one progression that breaks down in each subject and agree what the grade below teaches and what the grade above checks on arrival.

items.text: What do students carry from Grade 5 into Grade 6, and from Grade 8 into Grade 9, and who checks the hand-over?
items.data: 46 hand-over gaps; Grade 6 has 29 progression findings, the most of any grade
items.step: We could ask each school to name the 5 things it most needs students to arrive with, and share them with the school below.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: What does "taught in depth" look like in practice in Grade 2, and is it the same thing Grade 3 had in mind?
items.data: Grade 2 is 55% in depth and Grade 3 is 2%, a 53-point gap between neighbours
items.step: We could have neighbouring grades meet once a term to rate 5 shared standards together and compare what "in depth" means.

k-5.title: Part 2. Elementary, K-5
k-5.intro:
In K-5, teachers reported that 63% of the 700 grade-level ratings are at least introduced, and 21% are taught in depth. Grade 2 has the highest share in depth of any grade, and Math and Science lead the band at 29% each.

| Share in depth | K | G1 | G2 | G3 | G4 | G5 | K-5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Math | 26% | 42% | 62% | 0% | 21% | 32% | 29% |
| ELA | 0% | 21% | 71% | 0% | 7% | 18% | 19% |
| Science | 46% | 0% | 50% | 11% | 24% | 44% | 29% |
| Social Studies | 40% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 10% | 6% |
| All subjects | 16% | 21% | 55% | 2% | 12% | 24% | 21% |

items.title: Place value and Life Science are our strongest strands.
items.text: 60% of Number and Operations in Base Ten ratings are in depth, including every Grade 2 standard. In Science, Life Science is 47% in depth, Physical Science 31%, Earth and Space 25% and Engineering 11%.

items.title: Fractions are the thinnest Math strand.
items.text: None of the 30 fractions ratings in Grades 3 to 5 is in depth, and 63% are not taught. Operations and Algebraic Thinking, which also leads into middle school Math, is 23% in depth with 43% not taught.

items.title: Standards not taught in their own grade.
items.text: 222 K-5 standards are rated not taught in their own grade: ELA 100, Math 60, Social Studies 38, Science 24.

items.title: Progressions that break down.
items.text: 39 of 109 K-5 progressions break down on an official link, and 18 are taught at every step (11 of them in Science). Six Math progressions break down, from counting and place value to area and volume.

items.title: Introduced, never in depth.
items.text: 294 standards are introduced and never in depth: ELA 174, Math 63, Social Studies 29, Science 28. Grade 1 at least introduces 78% of its standards, the highest of any grade K-12.

items.title: Social Studies starts well and fades.
items.text: Kindergarten has 40% in depth. Grades 1 to 4 rated none of their Social Studies standards in depth, and Grades 2, 3 and 4 rate 73% to 89% not taught, perhaps because much of that time goes to literacy.

items.title: Many hand-over gaps begin in K-5.
items.text: 34 hand-over gaps begin in K-5 (Science 17, ELA 12, Social Studies 5). Nine of the Science ones, all on suggested links, start in K-5 Physical Science and feed Grade 8 and Grade 10 Physical Science.

items.title: Language is the thinnest ELA strand.
items.text: Language has 43 of the 100 ELA standards rated not taught in their own grade, and 52 of the 174 that are only introduced. Even Grade 2 Language is 31% in depth, against 78% to 100% for its other ELA strands.

items.title: Grade 3 may be teaching where students are.
items.text: Grade 3 rated most of its Essential Elements in depth (Math 59%, ELA 66%), while 31 of its 32 grade-level Math standards are rated not taught. One reading: teams teach in depth at the level students are at.

items.title: Power standards are not yet our most secure.
items.text: Power standards are 20% in depth, level with all standards (21%). Kindergarten names 47 of its 57 ELA standards as power, and Grade 3 rates 17 of its 18 Math power standards not taught.
How could each grade take its own grammar, conventions and vocabulary standards to depth?
items.data: K-5 Language is 10% in depth; Kindergarten Language is 93% not taught
items.step: We could choose each grade's 2 thinnest strands, such as Language, and plan one unit that takes them further.

items.text: What is Grade 2 doing that lets so much reach depth, and what could other grades borrow?
items.data: Grade 2 in depth: ELA 71%, Math 62%, Science 50%
items.step: We might ask Grade 2 to walk the K-5 team through how it plans a standard to depth.

items.text: Fractions begin in Grade 3 and feed ratios and algebra: what would a Grade 3 to Grade 6 plan for fractions look like?
items.data: 19 fractions standards not taught in their own grade; none in depth in Grades 3 to 5
items.step: We might plan one fractions sequence from Grade 3 to Grade 6, with a shared check at the end of each year.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: How can we embed Social Studies standards in the reading and writing we already teach in Grades 1 to 4?
items.data: No Social Studies standard rated in depth in Grades 1 to 4; not taught 57%, 74%, 89% and 73%
items.step: We could teach one Social Studies standard each term through a reading or writing unit we already run.

items.text: If Essential Elements are where much of our in-depth teaching sits, how do we plan from them up to the grade-level standard?
items.data: Essential Elements in depth: Math 82% against 29% for Math standards; ELA 46% against 19%
items.step: We might ask Grade 3 to share what it teaches below grade level, and how it plans from there to the grade-level standard.

g6-8.title: Part 3. Middle school, Grades 6-8
g6-8.intro:
In Grades 6-8, teachers reported that 61% of the 479 grade-level ratings (336 standards; each grade rates the same 64 Social Studies standards) are at least introduced, and 20% are taught in depth. ELA is the clear strength at 53%, with Grade 7 ELA at 70%.

| Share in depth | G6 | G7 | G8 | 6-8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Math | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| ELA | 40% | 70% | 50% | 53% |
| Science | 24% | 10% | 43% | 27% |
| Social Studies | 6% | 3% | 0% | 3% |
| All subjects | 17% | 22% | 21% | 20% |

items.title: ELA is strong in every strand.
items.text: Writing is 59% in depth, Speaking and Listening 58%, Reading 52% and Language 45%. Grade 7 Reading stands out at 89% in depth.

items.title: 52 standards are not taught in their own grade.
items.text: ELA 24, Social Studies 18 and Math 10. In Social Studies, Inquiry Practices, History and Political Science have no standard in depth in any grade (0 of 99 ratings).

items.title: Progressions: 12 break down, all in ELA.
items.text: 12 of the 48 ELA, Math and Science progressions here break down on an official link, and 15 are taught at every step. 3 Social Studies progressions are not taught in any of Grades 6, 7 and 8.

items.title: 159 standards are introduced but never in depth.
items.text: Math 71, Social Studies 40, ELA 38 and Science 10. In Math, Ratios and Proportional Relationships and Functions have no standard rated not taught.

items.title: Two ratings with almost no middle ground.
items.text: Grade 8 Science rated 43% in depth, 57% not taught and nothing introduced. Grade 7 Social Studies rated 91% of the 64 standards not taught, against 44% in Grades 6 and 8.

items.title: Math falls into middle school and rises out of it.
items.text: Math in depth is 32% in Grade 5, 0% in Grades 6 to 8 and 30% in Grade 9. Three Grade 9 Math standards taught in depth build, on official links, on Grade 6 and Grade 8 standards rated not taught.

items.title: Grade 6 is where most progression findings land.
items.text: Grade 6 has 29 findings, the most of any grade K-12, many of them Grade 6 standards that build on K-5 standards rated not taught. Across 6-8, 26 standards taught in depth build on such K-5 standards, on suggested links.

items.title: Middle school Math rated almost everything "introduced".
items.text: Each Math team rated all its standards, and none in depth. A pattern this uniform may reflect a strict reading of "ALL classes, all or nothing"; the teams can tell us.

items.title: Science looks organised by discipline.
items.text: Grade 6 carries Earth and Space (67% in depth), Grade 8 Physical Science (62%) and Grade 7 mainly Life Science (15%). 29 standards are not taught in the grade or course where they fit, mostly because that grade teaches another discipline.

items.title: Priority standards are deepest where teaching is already deep.
items.text: ELA priority standards are 68% in depth, above ELA as a whole (53%). Math priorities are rated like everything else (0%), and in Grade 7 Science 2 of 14 priorities are in depth and 6 not taught.
If Math introduces almost every standard, which 10 would we choose to take to depth first?
items.data: 71 Math standards introduced and never in depth; 10 not taught
items.step: We could choose 10 middle school Math standards to take to depth next year, starting with ratios and expressions.

items.text: When a grade teaches mainly one Science discipline, how are the standards from the other disciplines taught?
items.data: 29 Science standards not taught where they fit; Life Science 7% in depth and 67% not taught (K-5 47%, Grade 11 50%)
items.step: We could ask each Science grade to plan how it will teach the standards that fall outside its main discipline.

items.text: Could the Grade 5, middle school and Grade 9 Math teams rate 5 standards together and compare?
items.data: Math in depth: Grade 5 32%, Grades 6 to 8 0%, Grade 9 30%
items.step: We might bring the Grade 5, middle school and Grade 9 Math teams together to rate 5 shared standards.

items.text: Which K-5 standards does Grade 6 most rely on, and has Grade 6 told Grade 5?
items.data: 26 standards in depth in 6-8 build on K-5 standards rated not taught (suggested links)
items.step: We could ask Grade 6 teams to tell Grade 5 which K-5 standards they rely on most, checking each suggested link first.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: How is Social Studies scheduled across Grades 6 to 8, and where could its inquiry be taught alongside ELA?
items.data: Grade 7 rates 91% of the 64 standards not taught (Grades 6 and 8: 44%); 0 of 30 Inquiry ratings in depth
items.step: We might plan one Social Studies inquiry unit with ELA in each middle school grade, using ELA's strength in research and argument.

g9-12.title: Part 4. High school, Grades 9-12
g9-12.intro:
In Grades 9-12, teachers reported that 63% of the 575 grade-level ratings (377 standards) are at least introduced, and 28% are taught in depth, the highest of the three bands. ELA (51%) and Science (48%) are both strong, and Grade 10 Science has the highest share in depth of any grade and subject (79%).

| Share in depth | G9 | G10 | G11 | G12 | 9-12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Math | 30% | 14% | 5% | 6% | 14% |
| ELA | 33% | 49% | 60% | 60% | 51% |
| Science | 17% | 79% | 54% | 46% | 48% |
| Social Studies | 0% | 0% | 13% | 0% | 3% |
| All subjects | 24% | 32% | 34% | 23% | 28% |

items.title: Grade 10 Physical Science is all in depth.
items.text: All 15 Grade 10 Physical Science standards are in depth, and Grade 10 rates nothing not taught. Across the band, Physical Science is 88% in depth, Life Science 50%, Earth and Space 21%, Engineering 19%.

items.title: ELA reaches almost everything.
items.text: Only 14 of 180 ELA ratings are not taught, and 21 of 29 ELA progressions are taught at every step. Speaking and Listening is 100% in depth in Grades 11 and 12.

items.title: Only 7 standards are confirmed gaps.
items.text: These 7 are not taught in any grade or course they belong to. A further 119 are not taught in the grade or course where they fit: Math 77, Social Studies 22, Science 20.

items.title: Social Studies has 3 of 106 ratings in depth.
items.text: All 3 are in Grade 11 Economics, and Grade 10 rates 82% not taught. All 10 Inquiry standards are rated not taught in both Grade 9 and Grade 10.

items.title: 128 standards are introduced but never in depth.
items.text: Math 52, Social Studies 36, ELA 29 and Science 11. In Math, 11 of 21 strands have no standard in depth.

items.title: Math depth thins after Grade 9, priorities too.
items.text: Math falls from 30% in depth in Grade 9 to 6% in Grade 12, while ELA rises from 33% to 60%. Priority Math is 75% in depth in Grade 9, 41% in Grade 10, then 13% and 9%.

items.title: Grade 9 is a landing year.
items.text: From Grade 8 to Grade 9, ELA falls from 50% in depth to 33% and Science from 43% to 17%, while Math rises from 0% to 30%. In ELA, Grade 9 introduces and Grade 10 deepens: they agree on only 18 of the 43 standards both rate.

items.title: Some strong teaching rests on earlier gaps.
items.text: 20 standards taught in depth build on an earlier-school standard rated not taught: ELA 9, Science 6, Math 3, Social Studies 2. Only the 3 in Math rest on official links; 5 of the 6 in Science are Physical Science.

items.title: Language is the thinnest ELA strand again.
items.text: 30% in depth, against 54% to 69% for the other strands. It is also the thinnest strand in K-5 (10%).

items.title: Our deepest Math is algebra, a large part of SAT Math.
items.text: In Grade 9, The Real Number System is 100% in depth, Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities 60% and Creating Equations 50%. Other SAT areas are thinner: data and statistics at or near 0%, geometry and trigonometry under 10% apart from Congruence (31%).
Which Math standards do our students most need for the SAT and the diploma, and are those the ones we take to depth?
items.data: Algebra about 28% in depth; data analysis about 3%; geometry and trigonometry about 7%
items.step: We might map high school Math against the SAT areas and choose which thin strands to deepen first.

items.text: For the 119 standards not taught in the grade or course where they fit, which should each course take on, and who decides?
items.data: Math 77, Social Studies 22, Science 20; only 7 confirmed gaps
items.step: We could agree, course by course, which standards each course owns and which it leaves out on purpose.

items.text: What would help Grade 9 feel less like a restart in ELA and Science?
items.data: Grade 9 Writing 15% in depth (Grade 10: 77%); ELA and Science both dip from Grade 8
items.step: We might ask Grade 8 and Grade 9 teachers in ELA and Science to plan the first unit of Grade 9 together.

items.text: What should middle school know about what high school finds on arrival?
items.data: 3 Grade 9 Math standards in depth build on Grade 6 and Grade 8 standards rated not taught
items.step: We could share with middle school the 5 algebra ideas Grade 9 Math relies on most.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: Is Language (grammar, usage, vocabulary) taught through writing in high school, and would teams rate it differently if so?
items.data: Language 30% in depth; other ELA strands 54% to 69%
items.step: We could ask each ELA team whether Language is taught through its writing, and how that shows in its ratings.

math.title: Part 5. Math, K-12
math.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 62% of the 460 Math ratings (406 standards) are at least introduced, and 17% are taught in depth. Math has real peaks: Grade 2 (62% in depth), place value in K-5 (60%) and Grade 9 equations (60%).

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 | 173 | 29% | 36% | 35% |
| 6-8 | 81 | 0% | 88% | 12% |
| 9-12 | 206 | 14% | 35% | 51% |
| K-12 | 460 | 17% | 45% | 38% |

items.title: Number work and Grade 9 equations stand out.
items.text: Place value is 100% in depth in Grade 2, 75% in Grade 5, 63% in Grade 1. Grade 2 Operations and Algebraic Thinking (4 of 4), Grade 4 Geometry (3 of 3) and Grade 9 The Real Number System are fully in depth.

items.title: Fractions are not in depth in Grades 3 to 5.
items.text: 0% in depth across Grades 3 to 5. Not taught: 100% in Grade 3, 42% in Grade 4, 64% in Grade 5.

items.title: 70 standards are not taught in their own grade.
items.text: 60 are in K-5 and 10 in 6-8, most in Fractions (19), Operations and Algebraic Thinking (15) and Measurement and Data (15). In high school, 77 standards are not taught in the course where they fit best.

items.title: 10 of 18 progressions break down.
items.text: Each breaks down on an official Coherence Map link (a published map of which Math standards build on which); ratios is taught at every step. Three Grade 9 standards in depth build on Grade 6 or 8 standards rated not taught (official links).

items.title: 186 standards are introduced, never in depth.
The road from arithmetic to algebra is thin.
items.text: Fractions (Grades 3 to 5), ratios (introduced only in Grades 6 and 7) and expressions and equations have no standard rated in depth from Grade 3 to Grade 8. Each depends on the one before.

items.title: Grade 3 is a hinge year.
items.text: Multiplication, division, fractions and area all begin in Grade 3. Six progression findings land there, the most of any grade in Math, and 4 of the 10 broken progressions trace back to Grade 3 standards rated not taught.

items.title: Whole grades rated almost the same way.
items.text: Grade 3 rated 31 of 32 standards not taught, and middle school 71 of 81 introduced (its Essential Elements 7% in depth). Uniform ratings across a grade can say as much about the reading of the scale as about each standard.

items.title: K-5 Essential Elements tell a second story.
items.text: 82% of K-5 Math Essential Elements are in depth (95% in Grades 1 and 5). Deep Math teaching for students working below grade level may be happening at that level, which the grade-level ratings do not show.

items.title: High school Math narrows by design or by default.
items.text: Vectors, complex numbers, trigonometric functions and probability for decisions have little or nothing; several are advanced strands not every pathway includes. On the SAT road, algebra is strongest (about 28% in depth), data analysis (about 3%) and geometry and trigonometry (about 7%) thinner.
Which 10 Math standards per grade would we protect if we could only take 10 to depth?
items.data: 17% of Math in depth K-12; 186 standards introduced and never in depth
items.step: We could agree a short list of Math standards per grade that every class takes to depth, protected in the timetable.

items.text: Which high school strands have we chosen not to teach, and does each student's pathway still reach what the SAT asks?
items.data: 51% of high school Math not taught; 11 of 21 strands have nothing in depth; 77 standards not taught in the course where they fit
items.step: We could name the high school strands we have chosen not to teach and check each pathway against what the SAT asks.

items.text: What would Grade 5 and Grade 6 teachers each want the other to see in their classrooms?
items.data: Grade 2 62%, Grade 3 0%, Grade 5 32%, Grades 6 to 8 0%, Grade 9 30% in depth
items.step: We might hold one moderation session for Grades 2, 3, 5, 6 and 9, each bringing a piece of student work on the same idea.

items.text: If we followed one student's path through fractions, ratios and equations from Grade 3 to Grade 9, where would it feel secure and where would it feel thin?
items.data: Fractions 0% in depth in Grades 3 to 5; ratios and expressions 0% in Grades 6 to 8; Grade 9 equations 60%; 3 official hand-over gaps into Grade 9
items.step: We could follow fractions, ratios and equations as one thread from Grade 3 to Grade 9, with each grade naming its part.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: What did each team mean by its ratings, and would all five teams read the scale the same way after talking it through together?
items.data: Grade 3 rated 31 of 32 not taught; middle school 71 of 81 introduced; 45% of Math ratings are introduced
items.step: We might talk the scale through together, with evidence of what "in depth" looks like in every class: a shared quiz, a common task, reteaching time.

ela.title: Part 6. ELA, K-12
ela.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 79% of the 652 ELA ratings (562 standards) are at least introduced, the widest coverage of any subject, and 35% are taught in depth. ELA accounts for more than half of all the in-depth ratings in the school (227 of 406).

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 | 340 | 19% | 51% | 29% |
| 6-8 | 132 | 53% | 29% | 18% |
| 9-12 | 180 | 51% | 42% | 8% |
| K-12 | 652 | 35% | 44% | 21% |

items.title: Grade 2 and Grade 7 are our ELA peaks.
items.text: Grade 2: Writing 100% in depth, Speaking and Listening 88%, Reading Foundational Skills 80%, Reading 78%. Grade 7: Reading 89%, Writing 69%, Speaking and Listening 63%, Language 62%.

items.title: Kindergarten rated all its standards, and none in depth.
items.text: 60% are not taught, including 93% of Language and 78% of Reading; this is where reading and writing begin. None of its 47 power standards is rated in depth.

items.title: 128 standards are not taught in their own grade.
items.text: 100 in K-5, 24 in 6-8 and 4 in 9-12. Language has 50 of them and Reading 29.

items.title: 21 of 33 progressions break down at some step.
items.text: 4 are taught at every step K-12 (21 of 29 in high school alone). 19 standards in depth build on an earlier school's standard rated not taught, all on suggested links, not official ones, so each is worth checking first.

items.title: 241 standards are introduced, never in depth.
items.text: 174 in K-5, 38 in 6-8 and 29 in 9-12. Language has 84 and Writing 59.

items.title: The build is not a straight line.
items.text: Grade 2 (71%) is followed by Grade 3 (0%) and Grade 4 (7%), with no change of school to explain it. Grades 9 and 10 rate the same 43 standards but agree on only 18: Grade 9 introduces and Grade 10 deepens.

items.title: Middle school is where progressions strain.
items.text: Twelve of 29 progressions break down in Grades 6 to 8, usually where a middle school standard in depth builds on a K-5 step rated not taught. Reading and research skills (text features, evidence for claims, inquiry projects) recur.

items.title: Language never fully catches up.
items.text: It is the thinnest strand in every band (10%, 45%, 30% in depth), and 5 of the 19 hand-over gaps start from Grade 4 Language standards. The literacy audit of weekly plans found grammar and vocabulary instruction regular in only one or two elementary grades.

items.title: Foundational reading stops being in depth after Grade 2.
items.text: It is 0% in depth from Grade 3 to Grade 5, yet many of our students may still be learning to read there. Phonics and fluency may be taught below grade level, which the Grade 3 to 5 standards would not show.

items.title: Grade 3 may teach more than its rating shows.
items.text: Grade 3 rated 66% of its Essential Elements in depth and none of its grade-level standards. Kindergarten and Grade 4 rated few in depth at either level (Essential Elements 8% and 6%), perhaps a stricter reading or a different planning approach.
How is each grade's Language (grammar, conventions, vocabulary) taught: on its own, or through reading and writing, and what would take it to depth?
items.data: Language 10%, 45%, 30% in depth by band; 50 of 128 not taught in their own grade; 84 of 241 introduced only
items.step: In each band, we could decide how Language is taught: on its own, or through reading and writing.

items.text: What happens in Grade 2 and Grade 7 ELA that we could describe, share and repeat?
items.data: Grade 2 71% and Grade 7 70% in depth; Grade 3 0% and Grade 9 33%
items.step: We might ask Grade 2 and Grade 7, 2 of our 3 ELA peaks, to share how they plan to depth with the grades around them.

items.text: What would a shared K-12 picture of "a strong writer at Awsaj" look like at Grades 2, 5, 8 and 12?
items.data: Writing in depth: Grade 2 100%, Grade 5 15%, Grade 8 62%, Grade 9 15%, Grade 10 77%, Grade 12 60%
items.step: We might build that picture with one shared piece of work at each of Grades 2, 5, 8 and 12.

items.text: Which Grade 4 and Grade 5 Language and Reading standards does Grade 6 most rely on?
items.data: 12 hand-over gaps start in Grades 4 and 5; 5 of them from Grade 4 Language standards (suggested links)
items.step: We could help Grades 4 and 5 learn which Reading and Language standards Grade 6 relies on most.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: How did Kindergarten and Grade 4 decide between "introduced" and "in depth", and would a shared example change any ratings?
items.data: In depth, main standards and Essential Elements: Kindergarten 0% and 8%, Grade 4 7% and 6%, Grade 3 0% and 66%, Grade 2 71% and 73%
items.step: We might rate one shared example together and see whether any ratings change.

science.title: Part 7. Science, K-12
science.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 35% of the 247 Science ratings (208 standards) are taught in depth, level with ELA as the highest in the school, and 58% are at least introduced. High school Physical Science (88% in depth) is one of the strongest strands in any subject.

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 (AERO Science) | 90 | 29% | 32% | 39% |
| 6-8 (NGSS) | 74 | 27% | 19% | 54% |
| 9-12 (NGSS) | 83 | 48% | 18% | 34% |
| K-12 | 247 | 35% | 23% | 42% |

items.title: Physical Science builds to 88% in high school.
items.text: Physical Science is 31% in depth in K-5, 40% in 6-8 and 88% in 9-12. In Grade 10, all 15 Physical Science standards are in depth.

items.title: Priority and power standards are deepest here.
items.text: 48% in depth, the highest of any subject: 37% in K-5, 50% in 6-8, 55% in 9-12. Grade 8 priorities are 85% in depth.

items.title: K-5 progressions connect where units exist.
items.text: In K-5, 11 of 31 progressions are taught at every step, the most of any K-5 subject. 7 of 40 progressions break down on an official link, all in K-5.

items.title: Standards not taught in their own grade.
items.text: 24 confirmed, all in K-5: Physical Science 12, Earth and Space 8, Engineering 2, Life Science 2. In Grades 6 to 12, 49 more are rated not taught in the grade or course where they fit.

items.title: Hand-overs from K-5.
items.text: 17 standards taught in depth in Grades 6 to 10 (11 middle school, 6 high school) build on a K-5 standard rated not taught. All rest on suggested links, not official ones.

items.title: Depth alternates from year to year.
items.text: High, low, high, low from Kindergarten to Grade 3, and again from Grade 6 to Grade 10. A unit-based plan could produce this pattern, which teams could confirm.

items.title: Life Science has a long quiet stretch.
items.text: Strong in K-5 (100% in Grades 2 and 4), then 0% in Grades 6 and 8 and 15% in Grade 7, before returning in Grade 11 (50%).

items.title: Science is often all or nothing.
items.text: A standard is usually in depth or not taught, perhaps because Science is planned in whole units. It has the fewest "introduced only" standards (49, against 105 to 241 in the other subjects).

items.title: Each secondary grade seems to own a discipline.
items.text: Grade 6 Earth and Space, Grade 8 Physical Science and Engineering, Grade 9 Earth and Space, Grade 10 Physical Science, Grade 11 Life Science, Grade 12 Physical Science. Standards outside a grade's discipline are rated not taught.

items.title: Engineering is taught in bursts.
items.text: It is 20% in depth K-12, with depth in Grade 8 (100%) and Grade 11 (75%). Shared across grade bands, it may be a strand no single grade feels it owns.
How might students keep meeting Life Science between Grade 5 and Grade 11?
items.data: Life Science 0% in depth in Grades 6 and 8, 15% in Grade 7, 50% in Grade 11
items.step: We might plan one Life Science unit for Grades 6 to 8.

items.text: How will the 49 standards that fall outside each grade's main discipline be taught?
items.data: 49 standards in Grades 6 to 12 not taught in the grade or course where they fit; no confirmed gaps in Grades 6 to 12
items.step: We could decide, course by course, which of the 49 standards to start teaching and which we choose not to use.

items.text: What makes Grade 10 Physical Science work so well, and what could other courses borrow from it?
items.data: Grade 10: all 15 Physical Science standards in depth, nothing not taught
items.step: We might ask Grade 10 Physical Science to share what makes its units work with the Grade 4, 5 and 8 teams.

items.text: Which K-5 Physical Science ideas do Grade 8 and Grade 10 most rely on, and how could the K-5 grades they belong to teach them?
items.data: 12 K-5 Physical Science standards not taught in their own grade; 9 hand-over gaps run from them into Grades 8 and 10
items.step: We could have each K-5 grade start teaching its own Physical Science standards that Grade 8 and Grade 10 build on.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: Do we have a K-12 map of which Science units run in which year, and does it match what the ratings show?
items.data: Standards mostly either in depth or not taught; 49 introduced-only standards, the fewest of any subject
items.step: We could draw one K-12 map of which Science units run in which year, so every strand has a planned home.

social-studies.title: Part 8. Social Studies, K-12
social-studies.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 40% of the 395 Social Studies ratings (225 standards) are at least introduced, and 4% are taught in depth. It is the subject where a few shared choices could make the biggest difference, and it has clear starting points: Kindergarten (40% in depth) and an Economics thread in Grades 6 and 11.

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 (AERO Social Studies) | 97 | 6% | 30% | 64% |
| 6-8 (Wisconsin) | 192 | 3% | 38% | 59% |
| 9-12 (Wisconsin) | 106 | 3% | 39% | 58% |
| K-12 | 395 | 4% | 36% | 60% |

items.title: Economics and Kindergarten are the bright spots.
items.text: Economics holds 6 of the 15 in-depth ratings (3 in Grade 6, 3 in Grade 11). Four of Kindergarten's 10 standards are in depth, in identity, time and connections.

items.title: Standards not taught in any grade they belong to.
items.text: 59 confirmed (K-5 38, 6-8 18, 9-12 3). A further 46 are rated not taught in the grade or course where they fit.

items.title: Strands with no standard rated in depth.
items.text: K-5: Government, Culture, Production and Consumption, and Science, Technology and Society. Grades 6 to 12: Inquiry Practices (70 ratings), History (60) and Political Science (44).

items.title: Progressions break down mostly in K-5.
items.text: 21 of 64 break down: 15 break at a K-5 grade (mostly Grade 2 or Grade 3) and 6 in Grades 6 to 12. None is yet taught at every step.

items.title: Priority and power standards.
items.text: 5% in depth and 55% not taught, across 183 ratings. In Grade 7, 94% of priority standards are not taught.

items.title: Social Studies is consistent across the whole school.
items.text: Unlike the other subjects, it does not rise or dip by band. This looks like a whole-school pattern, not the story of any one team.

items.title: Economics also holds most hand-over gaps.
items.text: 5 of the 7 hand-over gaps sit in Economics: 3 Grade 6 Economics standards build on K-5 standards rated not taught, and 2 Grade 11 standards build on Grade 6.

items.title: The subject is introduced, rarely deepened.
items.text: Where Social Studies is taught, it is rated "introduced" about 9 times for every 1 time "in depth" (142 against 15). Review and assessment across all classes may be what is missing for "in depth".

items.title: Few shared standards reach depth in any grade.
items.text: Middle school standards belong to all three grades, and high school standards span several courses: 80 of 86 shared standards reach depth nowhere. When a standard belongs to everyone, each grade may leave it to another.

items.title: High school looks organised by course.
items.text: Grade 9 Geography (92% introduced), Grade 11 Economics (23% in depth), Grade 12 History (58% introduced). Standards outside each year's course show as not taught.
Which 5 to 8 Social Studies standards per grade matter most for our students in Qatar, and would we commit to taking those to depth?
items.data: 15 of 395 ratings in depth; each middle school grade rates 64 standards
items.step: We could choose 5 to 8 Social Studies standards in each grade to take to depth, and plan them into units we already teach.

items.text: Could Social Studies inquiry and ELA research be planned as one sequence from Grade 6 to Grade 12?
items.data: 0 of 70 Inquiry ratings in depth; Grades 9 and 10 rate all 10 Inquiry standards not taught; secondary ELA is over 50% in depth
items.step: We could start with one Grade 6 unit that counts for both subjects.

items.text: For standards shared across Grades 6 to 8, which grade introduces, which deepens and which assesses?
items.data: 80 of the 86 standards rated by 2 or more grades are in depth in none
items.step: We might ask Grades 6 to 8 to agree which grade introduces, deepens and assesses each shared standard.

items.text: Where does the AERO K-5 sequence hand over to the Wisconsin Grade 6 standards, and who should map it?
items.data: 5 hand-over gaps run from K-5 into Grades 6 and 7, all on suggested links not yet checked by teachers
items.step: We could ask K-5 and Grade 6 teachers to check the 5 suggested links together.
items.cat: Knowing the bands above and below

items.text: Do our priority and power lists match what our units and courses teach, and if not, which should change?
items.data: 55% of 183 priority and power ratings not taught, against 18% to 20% in the other subjects
items.step: We could start with Grade 7 (17 of 18 not taught) and Grades 2 and 3, keeping the standards our units already teach.

method.title: Method, sources and limits
method.intro:
Every figure in this paper was computed from the ratings sheet and cross-checked against the site. Where the site's band and K-12 views differ (progressions), the paper says which it uses. Percentages are rounded half up, as on the site.

**What was read**

| Source | How it was used | How fully it was read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ratings sheet, "All Standards and Ratings K-12" (9 Nov 2026) | Every figure | All 2,166 rows |
| Organized ratings workbook | Cross-check of totals | All tabs |
| 20 Findings decks (band and subject) | Cross-check, questions and next-step themes | All slides and speaker notes |
| K-12 Reports PDF (118 pages) | Cross-check | First 80 pages scanned by search; a few read directly |
| 7 other Reports PDFs | Cross-check of headline figures | Scanned by search, not read page by page |

**How terms are used**

- **Rated standards.** One rating is one standard in one grade. A standard shared by several grades is counted once for each grade that rated it.
- **At least introduced.** Rated in depth or introduced.
- **Not taught where it belongs (confirmed).** The grade the standard belongs to rated it not taught (for a standard shared across grades, every grade that shares it did). In Math and ELA each standard belongs to one grade, so this means that grade's team rated it not taught; it does not mean other grades should have taught it.
- **Not taught where it fits.** Each standard was placed in the grade or course where it fits best, and that grade or course rated it not taught. Other grades were not asked to rate it.
- **Introduced, never in depth (met but not owned).** Introduced in at least one grade and in depth in none.
- **Progression finding.** An automatic check on a chain of linked standards: a step not taught, or a standard in depth while the one it builds on is not taught.
- **Taught at every step.** Every standard in the chain, across two or more grades, is at least introduced.
- **Progression.** A chain of linked standards across grades. Official links are the Coherence Map (Math), anchor standards (ELA) and the standards' own structure (Science, Social Studies). Other links are suggestions.
- **Curricular capacity.** The average number of standards one grade rated in depth, introduced and not taught in a year (all ratings divided by the number of grades), rounded.
- **Hand-over gap.** A standard taught in depth while a standard it builds on, placed in an earlier school, is rated not taught.
- **Priority and power standards.** Standards the school's own documents name: power standards in K-5, priority standards in 6-12.

**Limits to keep in view**

- Ratings are teachers' judgements of teaching across a grade. They are not observations and not student results.
- Grades may have read "in depth" differently. Uniform ratings across a whole grade are a reason to check how the scale was read; the paper points these out so teams can discuss them.
- Each team rated its own subject. Literacy taught in Science and Social Studies, and Math taught in Science, may not show in the ELA and Math ratings.
- Middle school Science and high school Math, Science and Social Studies standards were placed in the grade or course where each fits best. 24 K-5 Social Studies standards are also rated not taught in the grade where they fit.
- Band counts of progressions look only at steps inside the band, so they do not add up to the K-12 figure.
- Literacy audit figures come from the 2026 PK-5 literacy audit of weekly plans.
- Some strands have few standards in a grade, so a single rating can move a percentage a long way. Counts are given where this matters.
- Suggested links between standards (most ELA, Science and Social Studies hand-overs) have not been checked by teachers.

**Status.** This is a draft for the Vertical Alignment Committee. Each finding should be checked with the teams concerned before it is treated as settled. The planned review of weekly and unit plans (Part 2) will test many of these patterns against what is actually planned.

see.glance: An average grade in a year, by subject: green in depth, blue introduced, pink not taught, with the number of standards.
see.grades: One column per grade. The top number is the share taught in depth.
see.data: The five main facts. Each links to its data on the site.
see.patterns: What the facts show side by side. Possibilities to discuss, not conclusions.
see.questions: Five questions for teams, each with its data and a first step we could take.
see.ourpart: Options for what we could do, under four headings, each with the data behind it.

see.kpi: Four headline figures for this part: the share taught in depth, at least introduced and not taught, and how many ratings they come from.

whole.glance: Of the standards we teach, most are introduced rather than taken to depth. ELA and Science go deepest, and Social Studies is where we have the most room to grow.
whole.grades: Depth goes up and down from grade to grade rather than climbing steadily, so the hand-overs between grades matter.
whole.data: Clear strengths, and a few places to build.
whole.patterns: Depth, not coverage, is what changes, which points us toward choosing what to go deep on.
whole.questions: What we choose to protect, and how grades can work together.
whole.table: The gap between subjects is the widest thing in the table: 4% in depth in Social Studies against 35% in ELA and Science.

k-5.glance: K-5 introduces widely. Math and Science go deepest, and Social Studies is mostly rated not taught.
k-5.grades: Grade 2 shows how deep teaching can go. The grades around it rated far fewer standards in depth, which is worth talking about together.
k-5.data: The foundations are strongest in number (place value). Fractions, Language and Social Studies are the thinner threads.
k-5.patterns: Much deep teaching in K-5 may happen at the level students are at (the Essential Elements), which the main ratings do not show.
k-5.questions: What every child carries into Grade 6.
k-5.table: Grade 2 carries the most depth in three subjects, and Social Studies is light after Kindergarten. Each team can find its own cell.

g6-8.glance: ELA is the strength of middle school. Math covers almost everything and rated none of its standards in depth.
g6-8.grades: Each middle school grade has its own mix, and Science seems to give each grade its own discipline.
g6-8.data: Two very different pictures sit side by side: a good place to compare how teams read the scale.
g6-8.patterns: Many differences here may come from how courses are scheduled and how strictly "in depth" was read, not from how much is taught.
g6-8.questions: What students bring into middle school and carry on.
g6-8.table: ELA is strong in every middle school grade, while Math is mostly introduced and Social Studies is mostly rated not taught. Each team can find its own cell.

g9-12.glance: High school goes deepest of the three bands, led by ELA and Science.
g9-12.grades: ELA builds year on year, and Math is strongest in Grade 9. The picture is mostly about choices between courses.
g9-12.data: Few standards are missing everywhere. Most open questions are about which course teaches what.
g9-12.patterns: ELA's steady, planned sequence goes with high depth, and the SAT areas in Math deserve a closer look.
g9-12.questions: What every graduate should leave with.
g9-12.table: ELA grows through high school, Science peaks in Grade 10, and Math is strongest in Grade 9. Each team can find its own cell.

math.glance: Introduced is Math's most common rating (45%). Depth is strongest in K-5 and in Grade 9.
math.grades: Strong early grades and a strong Grade 9 frame the middle years, where Math is introduced rather than taken to depth.
math.data: Number is our strength. Fractions, ratios and equations, the path to algebra, are the thread to follow.
math.patterns: Following one idea, such as fractions to equations, across the grades shows where teaching may need more depth.
math.questions: A few Math standards to take deeper together, across grades.
math.table: Middle school introduces almost all its Math, and high school leaves the most not taught, possibly by course choice.

ela.glance: ELA has the widest coverage and the most in-depth ratings of any subject.
ela.grades: ELA grows strongly from K-5 into secondary, with a few grades that rated little in depth.
ela.data: Reading, writing and talk are strengths. Language (grammar and vocabulary) is the thread to strengthen, and much of it may be taught in other subjects.
ela.patterns: ELA shows what steady building across grades looks like, and that literacy also lives in Science and Social Studies.
ela.questions: Sharing what works in ELA, and who takes Language to depth.
ela.table: "Not taught" shrinks from 29% in K-5 to 8% in high school: by the end, ELA reaches nearly everything.

science.glance: Science is often all or nothing: a topic is either taught deeply or not taught that year.
science.grades: Depth changes from year to year, which may simply follow which units each grade runs.
science.data: When Science is taught, it is more often in depth than introduced. The open question is which year each topic lives in.
science.patterns: Much of "not taught" in secondary Science is standards outside the discipline each grade teaches, and Science also carries a lot of literacy.
science.questions: A shared K-12 map of Science units, so every strand has a home.
science.table: Each band takes between a quarter and a half of its Science to depth. Middle school leaves the most not taught, mostly standards outside each grade's discipline.

social-studies.glance: Social Studies is mostly introduced. This is where a few shared choices could make the biggest difference.
social-studies.grades: Kindergarten starts strongly. After that Social Studies is mostly introduced, perhaps because much of the time goes to literacy.
social-studies.data: Many topics are at least introduced across the school, and Economics shows what a thread taught to depth can look like.
social-studies.patterns: Social Studies may be where much of our literacy happens, so planning the two together could help both.
social-studies.questions: A few Social Studies standards per grade to take deeper, often through literacy we already teach.
social-studies.table: The same pattern holds in every band: about four in ten at least introduced and very little in depth.
